title: Physiological Effects of Touching Coated Wood
research_question: To clarify the effects of touching wood with different coatings with the palm on left and right prefrontal cortex activity (assessed using near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy) and on autonomic nervous activity (assessed using heart rate variability and heart rate).

participants.description: 18 female university students (mean age, 21.7 ± 1.6 years) from Japan. Excluded smokers, those in treatment for disease, and those with menstrual period during the study period.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but likely university students from Chiba University.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Five types of white oak wood plates (length 300 × width 300 × thickness 43 mm) with different surface coatings: (1) uncoated, (2) oil-finished, (3) vitreous-finished, (4) urethane-finished, and (5) mirror-finished. All materials were kept at room temperature.

measures.instrument: Near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy (TRS-20 system; Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.)
Heart rate variability (ln(HF)) from electrocardiograph (Activtracer AC-301A)
Heart rate variability (ln(LF/HF)) from electrocardiograph (Activtracer AC-301A)
Modified semantic differential (SD) method (13-point scale for comfortable-uncomfortable, natural-artificial, relaxed-awakening, warm-cold, uneven-flat, dry-moist)

mechanisms: Physiological functions of modern day humans are best adapted to natural environments or materials, leading to relaxation when exposed to nature-derived stimuli (back-to-nature theory).

Differing physical properties of coatings (e.g., surface roughness and heat flow rate) influence tactile perception and subsequent physiological responses. Oil and vitreous finishes retain the texture of natural wood, contributing to physiological relaxation.
implementation_implications: The findings provide a scientific basis for the use of natural or near-natural coated wood in built environments to induce physiological relaxation.
Using uncoated, oil-finished, or vitreous-finished wood in indoor environments may contribute to preventive medical effects by promoting relaxation.

tables.description: Details of materials including thickness, thermal conductivity, arithmetic average roughness, and application rate of coatings.

limitations: The study only examined the effect of contact with the palm of the hand, not other body surfaces (e.g., sole of the foot, relevant for flooring materials).
The study only measured physiological effects by passive contact (placing the palm on the stimulus), not more active forms of contact (e.g., stroking).
Study participants were exclusively female university students in their twenties, limiting generalizability to other demographics (males, children, elderly).

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This study examined the physiological effects of touching wood with various coating with the palm of the hand on brain activity and autonomic nervous activity. Participants were 18 female university students (mean age, 21.7 ± 1.6 years). As an indicator of brain activity, oxyhemoglobin concentrations were measured in the left and right prefrontal cortices using near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy. Heart rate variability (HRV) and heart rate were used as indicators of autonomic nervous activity. The high-frequency (HF) component of HRV, which reflects parasympathetic nervous activity, and the low-frequency (LF)/HF ratio, which reflects sympathetic nervous activity, were measured. Plates of uncoated, oil-finished, vitreous-finished, urethane-finished, and mirror-finished white oak wood were used as tactile stimuli. After sitting at rest with their eyes closed for 60 s, participants touched the stimuli with their palm for 90 s each. The results indicated that tactile stimulation with uncoated wood calmed prefrontal cortex activity (vs. urethane finish and mirror finish), increased parasympathetic nervous activity (vs. vitreous finish, urethane finish, and mirror finish), and decreased heart rate (vs. mirror finish), demonstrating a physiological relaxation effect. Further, tactile stimulation with oil- and vitreous-finished wood calmed left prefrontal cortex activity and decreased heart rate relative to mirror-finished wood.
